subsubtopic: JOB LAY-OFFS AT DE HAVILLAND-BOEING LAWSUIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has just been announced that 700 jobs are being cut from the workforce of the de Havilland STOL aircraft plant in my riding at Downsview, Ontario. This is our major employer and a big part of Canada's aerospace industry.
Although the company claims that attrition can cover these jobs, the local union, Local 112 of the Canadian Auto Workers, tells me that this is impossible.
Since the Government sold the company to Boeing of Seattle there is less that it can do on behalf of Canadian workers. I call on the Government to review the lay-off decisions, no doubt made south of the border in Seattle, to defend these jobs and to assist employees who are affected.
We also have news of Boeing's $110 million lawsuit to cover false representations by the Government of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on the sale involving safety and health conditions. If Boeing is successful, since the company was sold for $90 million, the result will be that Boeing gets the company from the Canadian taxpayers free.
I submit that the Government should have known of the safety and health conditions since every worker in the plant knew of them. The Government is responsible for this give-away.

subsubtopic: TAX AND CHILD CARE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and this House the blatant unfairness of the income tax provisions and lack of child care provisions in this Budget for a single working mother in my riding of Mission-Coquitlam.
This woman who earns $1,400 per month has expenses in excess of $2,100 per month. She currently receives the family allowance of $65 a month and child support of $400 a month, yet she is $200 short at the end of the month. Her largest single expenditure is $850 per month for the care of her children while she is at work.
How is it that the Government claims that its tax and child care provisions are fair, yet this woman and thousands like her are being penalized by the unfairness of the Income Ihx Act and by child care being put on hold? She is not looking for charity. She is demanding fairness.
I call upon the Government to act immediately to redress this unfairness. I also call upon the Government to put real fairness in the tax system and acknowledge that working people of the country are being driven into debt by its taxation and child care policies.

subsubtopic: PRIVATIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the provincial and federal governments are selling their companies to private enterprise, to the socialists' great despair, communist countries are doing the same thing. But there, Mr. Speaker, it is even worse. They want to sell to foreigners. The Hungarians have just offered the Germans 53 companies, including large steel mills. The Germans are demanding guarantees, because to make these money losers pay, massive lay-offs will be necessary. Mr. Speaker, the Canadian NDP should give us such news from time to time.

May 3, 1989

subsubtopic: VISIT TO OTTAWA OF YULI KOSHAROVSKY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Yuli Ko-sharovsky first submitted his emigration application to leave the Soviet Union in 1971. A radio engineer, Kosharovsky was not allowed to work in his profession after he applied. He held a number of jobs, including those of night watchman and manual labourer.
Yuli's wife Inna is a mathematician with a degree from Moscow State University. She too was prevented from working in her field.
Because of his active involvement to spread Jewish culture and to teach Hebrew, Yuli was branded a traitor. As recently as 1987 when I met Yuli in Moscow, it was stated in a leading Moscow paper that he would never be allowed to leave, for reasons of state secrecy.
However, late last year, Yuli's prayers were answered. He and his family were granted exit visas and they arrived in Israel on March 12, 1989. Their 18-year struggle is over.
Mr. Kosharovsky is in Ottawa today to share his experiences and to urge the Canadian Government to continue to pressure the Soviet Union to live up to its human rights obligations.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was my intention to speak about the way in which the Budget has had a devastating effect upon my own riding and upon western Canada. However, with the announcement today of our Leader's resignation, I want to take this opportunity to say something in a personal way about the man I have known for over 25 years in public life.
Over that time he has been for me a great teacher and mentor, especially about this House of Commons and about the meaning of Parliament in Canada. As a Member of Parliament from western Canada he has spoken well and effectively about the interests of our region. Particularly as Leader of our Party he has fought
to preserve the independence of the country, and in the last election it was with great pride that we served with him.
As a friend and associate he will be missed. As a person who can give us the real sense of the House of Commons he will be missed. As a Member from western Canada he will be missed. As a national Leader he will be long remembered for the fight and choice he gave Canadians back in November 1988.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO MEMBERS OF POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to a group of citizens who have been working tirelessly in the name of a supreme issue, that is, the environment.
These volunteers who have come together under the banner of POWER which stands for Protect Our Water and Environmental Resources, have recently been named citizen of the year by the Acton Chamber of Commerce.
Members of POWER, which include Ruth French, Ken McGregor and hundreds of others, have succeeded in raising public awareness of key environmental issues.
These citizens know the future lies in recycling, recovering, reusing and rethinking the way we treat our environment.
They oppose further landfill sites, particularly the establishment of one in a dangerous quarry location with the potential to pollute the groundwater for thousands of people in my riding. I stand behind the citizens and these environmentalists.

subsubtopic: B.C. INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today in Vancouver there is a gathering of people whose livelihoods depend on the B.C. fishing industry. This rally is to protest the new Conservative regulations which will gut the Canadian industry of its fish and its jobs. New Democrats support those workers.
May 3, 1989

Our fishing industry has never been threatened like it is today. American interests want our herring, want our salmon and want our jobs.
Over the last three years, the current Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) and the former Minister for International Trade made repeated promises to this House that Canada would fight the U.S. complaint to GATT, that B.C. fish would be landed, inspected and gutted in Canada, and that Canadian natural resources and Canadian jobs would be protected.
None of those promises were kept. Those Ministers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have sold out the B.C. fishing industry to the Americans. The Americans are still not satisfied. They feel that the landing requirements would bruise their fish. The Americans already believe they own our fish.
Where are our rights to grade our fish and to gut our fish, our rights to Canadian resources, and our rights to our jobs? Americans must not be allowed to steal our natural resources with or without the connivance of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: LIBERAL POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Harb) applauded a decision to reduce Department of Transport expenditures by some $200 million, thereby contradicting his caucus.
Certainly, the Liberals have never understood Canada and never will. That explains their increasingly negative position on the Meech Lake Agreement.
In their caucus, the Liberals do not even agree on the National Capital Commission, the Ottawa-Hull region, which is only a part of Canada. How will they be able to agree on a national consensus on the Meech Lake Agreement?

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to have represented the new riding of Carleton-Gloucester since last November. It is also
an honour for me to represent part of the riding formerly represented by the Right Hon. John TUmer.
A man of courage and integrity, he devoted his energies to his country's business.

As a Member of Parliament representing ridings in Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) served his electors and all Canadians with great enthusiasm and determination.
As defender of the unity of Canada, he was a courageous, decent person and a true Canadian. The future will prove that the Right Hon. Member should have been our present Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: IMPROVEMENT OF SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to give the people in my riding who are now receiving unemployment insurance benefits or who may do so in the future that the Government will continue to help those who lose their jobs.
The improved system will take into account the dynamic nature of our regional economy. The Unemployment Insurance Program has simply been adjusted to the vitality of our regions. The old system was obsolete, Mr. Speaker. We are now adjusting to the economic situation as it is today.
The entrepreneurial spirit of the people of Beauce has already created many jobs, and the Department of Employment and Immigration will provide retraining and skills upgrading for those who need it. An additional $800 million has been earmarked for retraining. The new formula is still just as generous for benefit recipients. Benefit amounts have been maintained. It makes good sense to adjust the Unemployment Insurance Program to the economic circumstances in Beauce and elsewhere. Contributors to the Unemployment Insurance Fund will realize that the new system will be fairer, more equitable and more effective.
Furthermore, as the Member for Beauce, I intend to defend the interests of all those constituents who are receiving or who will receive unemployment insurance benefits.

May 3, 1989
Tribute to Right Hon. John Turner

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

In view of announcements that were made this morning, we are going to hear members of all Parties with respect to the announcement of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition.
I first of all call upon the Deputy Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Government of Canada, colleagues here in the House, and all members of the Progressive Conservative Party to pay tribute to my friend, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) who just this morning has announced his intention to resign as Leader of the Liberal Party.
As we watched the right hon. gentleman over the past week, and despite Ottawa being awash with rumours of an impending resignation, many of us on this side of the House had come to the conclusion that maybe he was going to put it off until the next time February 29 rolled around. I guess, as usual, his good sense and good judgment prevailed, and he did what he considered to be the right thing this morning.
It is at times like this when this institution, the House of Commons, demonstrates that it is a very special place, a very unique place. As a gentleman whom the right hon. gentleman admired so much, the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, used to say on various occasions like this one, "Parliament lives".
Today we recognize that it is truly a living institution and that it always rises to the occasion, for it was just yesterday that the right hon. gentleman engaged in a very vigorous debate as is his responsibility as Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition and today we are here in this House to set aside our differences and pay tribute to him as ;a distinguished parliamentarian and as an outstanding Canadian.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
As a parliamentarian he has indeed had a long and remarkable career. He was first elected to the House of Commons in 1962 and re-elected on seven different occasions. It was during this time that he served
ridings in three different provinces, the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia. As one who has known the right hon. gentleman for over 20 years, I have always admired his respect for this institution, his desire to preserve its integrity to ensure that the uniqueness and integrity of this institution be preserved as the basic pillar of freedom and democracy in this Canada of ours.
He did so frequently, he did so eloquently, and he did it with vigour, while at the same time he used those parliamentary instruments to his advantage and to his Party's advantage in the best parliamentary tradition.
I think it is fair to say that the right hon. gentleman had an intense respect for all Members of the House of Commons. I remember that when I came here as a back-bencher he was the Minister of Justice. He always tried to respond to the questions that were asked and he always considered the requests of MPs as a priority.
In government he held many portfolios which reflected his broad interests and his abilities-Registrar General, Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Solicitor General, Minister of Justice, Minister of Finance, and Prime Minister. That is a record that all Hon. Members I am sure would agree has been matched by few.
Above all, I am sure that it is fair to say that all Canadians admired his tenacity and strength of character as he fought in difficult and trying circumstances for what he felt was the interests of his Party and for his vision of Canada. His life outside this theatre and outside politics was equally distinguished. As a Rhodes Scholar, a prominent and successful lawyer and as a businessman, he brought the same characteristics he displayed in the House of Commons to the other facets of his life.
We note with some satisfaction as well that he was a noted author. He wrote a book called The Politics of Purpose wherein he talked about the exports of water, something which came in quite useful during the free trade debate from time to time. John Diefenbaker said: "Never write a book until you are almost through. It will come back to haunt you".
In the best spirit and in keeping with the best parliamentary tradition, on behalf of the Prime Minister, the Government, my colleagues and our Party, we extend to the right hon. gentleman, his wife Geills and his family enjoy what will obviously be a less hectic and more relaxing pace. We wish you well, Sir.
May 3, 1989

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I held a rather innocent press conference a few weeks ago, I had no idea I would be setting a veritable trend, and I do not know where the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is but I am sure we will learn about that later today.
More seriously, I am absolutely delighted to join with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) on behalf of my colleagues to pay tribute to a very distinguished parliamentarian and a very exceptional Canadian.

The Right Hon. Member has served as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Minister of Finance and Minister of Justice. He has been Solicitor General, Leader of the Opposition and Prime Minister of Canada.
As Minister of Justice, he sponsored the reform of the Criminal Code.
As a New Democrat, I cannot truthfully say that I always agreed with him when he was Minister of Finance. In fact, those instances were few and far between. However, even during that period he made a number of good suggestions and on one occasion increased pension benefits.

Among the many attributes of the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra, for Hon. Members who have known him as have the Deputy Prime Minister and others, myself included, going back 20 years, a very special attribute, to use a phrase that he has used himself about others, is that the Hon. Member is very much a House of Commons man.
For me, there are two special connotations to that phrase. One is a person who has recognized the importance of the traditions of parliamentary democracy and, more relevant, has understood those traditions and has understood that they have not been perpetuated over time as mere ornaments but because they have given substance to our Parliament in terms of their application to real life democracy in this country of ours. He has well understood that, and I want to pay particular tribute to him as a Minister when he understood that in replying to
Tribute to Right Hon. John Turner
questions from this side of the House, as Prime Minister, and as Leader of the Opposition. He was an exceptional Member of Parliament who, perhaps more than any other Member during my time, has both understood and respected those parliamentary traditions.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: The second aspect is that it is a very human attribute. The man we are honouring today has not only been vigorous in debate, has not only well understood parliamentary traditions, but has well understood something that some of us tend to forget from time to time, that debate is important, that the expression of ideological and philosophical differences is very important and that is why we are here, but at the same time, he has had a great capacity for recognizing the independent dignity and worth of each Member of the House of Commons, regardless of his of her Party affiliation. It is important, he has expressed without necessarily saying it, to have vigorous partisan debate, but it is equally important to recognize the human dignity of each Member of this House beyond those partisan considerations.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first time the Right Hon. Member ran for the leadership of the Liberal Party, he cut a dashing figure as the anti-establishment candidate. This augured well for his future in his Party and his country. As the Leader of his Party, he has demonstrated what he so aptly said a few weeks ago after my own announcement, that politics is a tough game but an honourable calling.

His special qualities were evident for all to see in the House and outside the House when in spite of intense back pain he waged an exceptionally vigorous campaign during the recent election for the kind of independent Canada he so evidently believes in. Instead of adversity weakening him, it simply deepened his resolve.
On behalf of my colleagues, I salute a decent man, a serious politician. We wish him, Geills and the family well. Good luck in the future.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

May 3, 1989
Tribute to Right Hon. John Turner

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal caucus, and I think on behalf of Liberals all across this country, to pay tribute to a great Canadian and a great parliamentarian, our Leader, the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner). Today, Mr. Speaker, we thank him for his courage, his integrity, his ability and for his deep feelings for Canada. All of these have enabled him to give leadership, not just here in the House but across the country, in the fight for the kind of Canada he and we believe in, a sovereign, independent Canada, able to define and apply its own values of caring and concern for all of its people.
This battle did not end with a full victory for us under his leadership. But we believe it is not yet over. His commitment and his courage will inspire us to continue that battle until it is won.
On a more personal note, all of us, especially myself, appreciate his friendship and his encouragement. We also recognize his very distinguished parliamentary career which saw him, as Minister of Justice, take important steps in law reform, which saw him as Canada's first Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, which saw him as the Minister of Finance who began the concept of indexing of pensions and personal income tax, so important to Canadians today.
We pay tribute to the Leader of the Opposition today. We thank him for all he has done, and we wish him and his family happiness, health and contentment in the future. But we recognize with satisfaction that he will continue to lead us here in the House and across the country for some time yet with vigour and enthusiasm. We say to the Leader of the Opposition, we, your colleagues and friends, thank you for how far we have travelled together on the road to a better Canada. We say to him, thank you for the example of courage and commitment which will help us to continue to move forward.

Mr. Speaker, we say thank you for the encouragement, dedication and above all the courage of the Leader of the Opposition. And we can assure him that the battle will continue.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not perhaps very much one can add to the words of tribute that have been accorded to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) here today, but I think it would be fitting that one of his colleagues from British Columbia says a word of appreciation for the friendship that we have enjoyed together over many years.
I got to know the right hon. gentleman quite early. When I came here in 1972 he was the Minister of Finance and I recall my first question being directed to the right hon. gentleman. All of us who have gone through this experience know the nervousness and excitement that is associated with such a debut. Of course, my question was overly long and was perhaps a little too smart, and the Speaker cut me off. I was terribly embarrassed. I noticed that the right hon. gentleman sort of had a deep feeling for me, and he was kind enough-I never told him this because I never wanted him to feel that I was obligated to him-

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
-to take the time, Mr. Speaker, to wait until I left the House to move outside and meet me there. He congratulated me on my first question and wished me well. I have never forgotten that.
I got to know him better a few years later when, as fate sometimes plays tricks on us, we found ourselves in Labrador on a fishing trip next to a stream. The aircraft that brought us there and was to bring us back got into difficulty, and the right hon. gentleman fell in the river. We one had one fish, and his boots were full of cold water. The night was wearing on and we were in desperate straits. He has been telling the story around the country that he saved my life because fortunately he did have the matches that helped us light a fire, and he did catch the fish and had the libation that carried us through half the night.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Of course, I never told anyone that I saved his life because of the reaction I would have gotten from some of my friends on this side of the House, and even some on the other side.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Oh, Oh!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
The longer one serves in this institution, the more one discovers that it is just as difficult to leave politics as it is to get into it. It requires just as much courage to make the decision that the right hon. gentleman has made today, as to decide to get into politics and make the sacrifices that are associated with it.
May 3, 1989

I assume of course that the right hon. gentleman will move home to British Columbia and that he will contribute to the life and the progress of our province in his later years.
I want to say to him on behalf of all his friends and colleagues here in the House from British Columbia, and in fact on behalf of all British Columbians, thank you for the contribution you have made to Quadra, to our province, to the country; and to your family, all the very best in the future.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had to give some serious consideration as to measuring my words about retiring politicians considering my own circumstance. One could say, upon listening to the words said to a retiring politician, that they are blandishments to return. If indeed this is the case with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), I would second the motion. The Leader of the Opposition has been a servant of Canada and a servant of British Columbia in a number of particular ways that touch not only me personally, but the people of British Columbia. I want to publicly acknowledge the role that the Leader of the Opposition played in a major controversy at the time between British Columbia and Canada. I will not go into the details, but a decision was made in my office and, on the basis of a handshake, a policy was formulated. Within 18 months of that policy being formulated, it would have been to the advantage of the Government of the day and the Minister, now the present Leader of the Opposition, to go back on that handshake. It would have been understood if he did, but to this day that Member never once has gone back on a deal that he made as representative of the Crown.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition is a Member of the House of Commons from the old school. He has a sense of tradition, a sense of proportion and a sense of history. He got it from his mother, who was a great British Columbian, and as the Chancellor of the University of British Columbia was a champion for our province and the people of that province.
Tribute to Right Hon. John Turner
The Leader of the Opposition has served very well in representing his constituency in British Columbia, from a political point of view, only too well. But beyond that, Mr. Speaker, I value his personal friendship, I value his historic and sincere commitment to the Province of British Columbia, but more important, as a Canadian he saw British Columbia as part of Canada. He will be a great loss not only to British Columbia but to this Chamber.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the Liberal Caucus and through Caucus, on behalf of Liberals everywhere in Canada.
Today has been an emotional day for all of us. Indeed it has been a day of reflection as we pay tribute to a leader who took on his role in the history of the Liberal Party of Canada with great courage and integrity, a Party that has been among the most successful of political organizations in the free world. However, continued success demands renewal and we began that renewal in 1984. In 1984 some said that, after decades of political success, our Party was destined for oblivion. The last chapter of the Liberal Party of Canada had been written. With all due respect to the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), as recently as last fall a similar prediction was made.
Mr. Speaker, John Turner, by the force of his will, by the depth of his commitment and by the power of his passion turned back those predictions and leaves this Party today a dynamic and renewed organization all across Canada, and for that we thank him.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
We have a saying in Newfoundland that the measure of a captain is not how well he sails his ship in calm waters, but rather how well he sails his ship through the storm. Martin Luther King, Jr., put it another way. He said: "The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy."
Leader, on behalf of Liberals everywhere, I am proud to say that notwithstanding the moments of challenge and controversy, and Lord knows there have been a few of them, we were proud to stand with you, Sir, and we thank you for your contribution to Parliament, to our Party, and to the country.

May 3, 1989
Tribute to Right Hon. John Turner
On March 16, 1984, upon his return to public life, the Right Eton. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) stated: "I have always believed that every Canadian has a duty to serve our country. Public service is a high calling. It is a way I can give back to my country a small measure of what it has given me-I have no magic wand. I have no instant solutions. But I do make a pledge. I will make whatever sacrifices are necessary. I will devote myself to my country. I will not flinch from the tough decisions. You will know where I stand".
Those are not partisan words. They are the words of a proud son of Canada, and they are a challenge to every single one of us in this place. John Turner has lived up to the standard he set for himself. As Parliamentarians, we would all do well to seek to follow his example. We give our best to his wife, Geills, his family and, of course, to you, Leader.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Sunday, I had the opportunity to introduce the Right Hon. John Turner in Montreal. I would like to repeat today some of what I said: a man of courage, a man with presence, a great Parliamentarian, as the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker often said-and you know, John Diefenbaker was occasionally right-a man of principles, a man who through all sorts of challenges maintained his commitment to serving Canada, the ideal of Canada, what it represents for all of us, a different country, more free, more egalitarian and more humane.
Mr. Turner, you are deeply attached to Quebec, not only because some members of your family still have roots there, your sister Brenda has always lived in Montreal for-dare I say-more than 30 years, but also because you know that Quebec's place in Canada is unique and for all these years, you have always acted to guarantee this special position.
A man's strength of character is judged in adversity. I have been a living witness to it. Indeed, your patience, your composure during the difficult storms of these years, 1984 to 1989, and also the courage with which you bore and accepted a difficult physical condition during the last election campaign have earned you the respect and sympathy of all Canadians.
You gave your support to the Meech Lake Agreement and you never wavered in your decision, despite the unfavourable reaction this brought you from many quarters, and for this we thank you. You understood-I repeat-you understood that the Canadian federation is
always in the making. For this, we thank you and I thank you.
You began your political career in Montreal in 1962, as Member for Parliament for St. Lawrence-St. George, which helped you to become quite familiar with the distinct character of Montrealers and Quebecers.
Mr. Speaker, a politican is never alone in life, and on behalf of all Canadians, I wish to thank his wife Geills, as well as his children Elizabeth, Michael, David and Andrew for sharing him with us. Thanks!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Tbrner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will understand fully when I say that over the years I have found that the goodbyes in this place are far more generous and spontaneous than the hellos.
Notwithstanding, I am very touched by the words of three old friends of mine: the Deputy Prime Minister and Member of Parliament for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski), the Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), and my colleague and friend of 30 years, the Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), and particularly the reference to our shared mission in the House of Commons to which I will refer in a moment.

I must also thank my colleagues, the members of the caucus, the Hon. Member for Humber-St. Barbe- Baie Verte (Mr. Tobin) as well as the longest serving Member of the House, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), for their most generous words.

I was particularly touched by what the Minister of Forestry and the Member of Parliament for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) had to say, and the Member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca (Mr. Barrett). I consider it a privilege to represent our province and I am particularly sensitive to the way they address this House before your Honour.
I am not going to allow the record to stand unchallenged, however. I leave it to you, Mr. Speaker. You understand what it is to seek salmon on both coasts, and I want to tell the Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) the question before the House will always be: Who had the matches, who killed the salmon, who had the bottle?
May 3, 1989

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Who saved whom? Let it be a warning to any Member who ventures into the outdoors to go properly equipped.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that you are allowing me the indulgence of the House. We are interrupting the public time of the country, but before I address a few short matters I want to thank Geills and the family for all the support they have given me.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
I was extremely touched by what all Hon. Members said about the House of Commons, because for me as well as for everyone here, the greatest privilege for a Canadian is to be elected by his or her fellow citizens to the House of Commons. I always told my colleagues, especially the youngest ones: "Be careful, respect others." We must respect the other Members of whatever party because everyone here, each and every one of us, represents Canadians as a result of an election in a highly free country.

This is and remains the forum of the nation. This is the highest court in the land. This is the place where finally issues must be decided.
I know, from time to time, critics and members of the media and those who watch Question Period wonder what we are doing here. Yes, it should be a legislative workshop, as there is business to be accomplished on behalf of the people of Canada. But the word Parliament, taken from the Norman, was well chosen. This is theatre, this is debate. It is the freest Chamber in the free world.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
It is unruly at times, but it is untrammelled and uncensored, and unpredictable.
I had a very good question from Gail Morris in the press conference today. She asked me my impressions of what had changed during my years here. I think the most
Tribute to Right Hon. John Turner
fundamental influence, of course, is television as it reflects on the proceedings of the House. I welcome that change. I think we all do. It converts the House of Commons again into a town hall, a forum for the people.
But it has changed the elements of the House. You and I were talking about it, Mr. Speaker. Question Period has become the dominant issue and period of focus of the people as it relates to the House of Commons. I think we should recognize that. Perhaps it should be extended so that all Members of the House, particularly members on the Government side, can participate more fully in it. I think we ought to extend statements pursuant to Standing Order 31 to allow individual Members of Parliament to make their points of view.
I have always felt, to continue the excellent work of Jim McGrath, now the Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland and Labrador, that we ought to examine whether fewer issues remain issues of confidence so that there is more liberty of expression and freedom of registering our votes in this Chamber.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
I think there are ways of maintaining the relevance of this place, and increasing it, because it disturbs me that while the House is full during Question Period, as it properly should be, with Members from all sides of the House, the House is not as full as it might be during principal debates, the Throne Speech, the Budget and debate on second reading of principal pieces of legislation, reflecting the importance of issue we are debating here. There must be ways, under your guidance, that we can re-enhance the relevance of this place. I know how strongly you and I feel about it, Mr. Speaker.
In any event, the Member for Vegreville, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), mentioned the late John George Diefenbaker. I say this not in any pompous way, I hope, but I remind particularly our young Members of Parliament from all sides of the House that Mr. Diefenbaker used to say: "Don't neglect this place, spend your time here. It may take many years to build up a reputation in the House of Commons but you can lose it in one day". That is the importance of this place, and it is one place I am really going to miss.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

May 3, 1989
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Before we commence Question Period, I should point out that it will continue in just a moment for the usual 45 minutes.
I want to say something to a number of Members on both sides of the House who came to me and would have wanted very much to make an intervention on this occasion in which we have all joined together. It was my decision, of course, to finally say that perhaps, at least for now, we have heard all that is appropriate under the circumstances. As the right hon. gentleman we praised today pointed out, we have the business of the country to proceed with.
I would not remark on this very often, but I want to say to Hon. Members that given the hour there will have to be the absence of some members of the Cabinet because of prior obligations. I hope that under all the circumstances Hon. Members will exercise care and courtesy in not making a point of that.
However, we are running 45 minutes late now. Oral Questions.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: INCREASED TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you have urged, we will get back to the public business of the country. My question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Even in this Canada of ours, more than three million people live in poverty. Over one million children live in poverty, 40 per cent of single or widowed women live under the poverty line. When we should be helping to lift our fellow Canadians beyond the poverty line and out of poverty, how can the Minister justify the fact that since he has been Minister of Finance he has raised the taxes of people living at the poverty line by 60 per cent? Meanwhile, those with incomes of $100,000 have had an increase of only eight per cent. What kind of fairness does he think this represents and what kind of vision of Canada does he think it represents?

subsubtopic: INCREASED TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member will recall that-I do not have the figures right off the top of my head-some 250,000 or 300,000 fewer people are living under
the poverty line since we came to office in 1984. We have also introduced a number of changes that respond to the needs of these people. The refundable sales tax credit was something that was introduced by this Government and has been increased in two consecutive Budgets. We have also increased the value of the child tax credit. In a number of ways, we have responded to the needs of these people.
Finally, let me say that through tax reform we have taken 850,000 people who are at the lower end of the income scale off the tax rolls. Again, I think that demonstrates our concerns to which the Hon. Member refers.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: CUTS IN HEALTH CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, referring to the Minister's own figures as contained in five successive Budgets, the cumulative tax increase for a couple with one earner, two children, earning $23,600-which is the poverty line-over five years of his custody of the finances of this country has been 60 per cent.
As a result of this Budget, the federal Government will contribute $4 billion less through the provinces for health care and post-secondary education. How can the Minister justify fewer spaces and higher tuition fees for our colleges and universities? How can he justify longer lists of people waiting to get into our hospitals? How can he justify inevitably lower quality health care for Canadians?

subsubtopic: CUTS IN HEALTH CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have responded to questions along those lines in previous meetings of the House of Commons. I say to the Hon. Member, he has chastised me roundly for the increase in the debt of this country in recent years. He knows full well that the only way that you can stop the debt from growing is to get the annual deficit down to zero. I have yet to hear any alternatives from the Hon. Member as to how we will get that debt down to zero.
We have had criticism time and time again of the measures that we have taken, measures that are regarded by many commentators across this country as evenly spread, as balanced in their impact, and what we are trying to do is solve this debt problem so that we can maintain the very programs that the hon. gentleman himself is saying we should maintain.

May 3, 1989

Oral Questions

subsubtopic: CUTS IN HEALTH CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we recognize, as does the Minister, the problem of the public debt and the annual deficit and what he has contributed to it. We say to him that when he cuts both, "Don't do it on the backs of the weak, the unemployed or the weaker regions of the country or the handicapped." Don't do it that way.

subsubtopic: CUTS IN HEALTH CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, more than half of Canada's single mothers raise their children on incomes that are below the poverty line.
How can the Minister of Finance justicy cutbacks that are adding to the burden of families and children, and especially to that of our poorest provinces?
Why didn't he keep his promises to the neediest in this country.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is saying that we are hurting the provinces which are the poorest. We have kept in place the equalization program which goes specifically to the poorer provinces in the country.
There is a statute there you can't touch.

The Hon. Member says there is a statute there, we can't touch it. This House, and as the Hon. Member, a fine Parliamentarian, knows, laws can be changed, but we are respecting the needs of the provinces. We are respecting the needs of the provinces which are in the lower income areas of the country because of the very concerns that the Hon. Member has expressed. In this Budget we are bringing in a large corporations tax which will raise $1 billion, to be paid by large corporations. We brought in a high-income surtax, specifically to put a heavier burden on those parts of the country, those people, those companies that are best able to bear the burden.
Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, the primary objective of this Budget is to ensure that we can retain the services important to people with lower incomes and who are in the less well off regions of the country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday, Therese Lavoie-Roux, the Quebec Liberal Government's Minister responsible for family policy, attacked the Budget of the Minister of Finance, saying it was anti-family. She quoted items that make it an anti-family budget: recovery of family allowance; deindexation of family allowance; cutbacks in spending on health and education; and the new sales tax on new homes that will affect young couples.
Could the Minister inform the House why he brought down an anti-family Budget?

Mr. Speaker, I reject that commentary on the Budget. Family allowance cheques will be received by 100 per cent of the people who are eligible to receive them. That continues. The universal character is maintained. The Hon. Member refers to Established Programs Financing. That, as I said yesterday, will increase by $25 billion over the course of the next five years relative to the last five years.
Finally, his comments are quite wrong as they relate to the cost of housing. We have made a commitment which is repeated in the Budget papers which states that if there is an affordability problem, we will take action to offset that affordability problem. The details will be made known in the next few months.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister refuses to understand, refuses to admit that one of the major problems in Canada is our declining birthrate.
The Minister ought to realize, considering what it costs today to raise children, that we need a generous family policy, not a regressive one.
The Minister deindexed family allowance payments, and now he has started to recover those payments, starting at a certain income level. Today, he is going after people with high incomes. Next year, when he needs extra money, he will go down to $20,000 or $25,000.

May 3, 1989
Oral Questions
Could the Minister explain why he did not look at other ways of reducing his deficit instead of going after Canadian families?

Mr. Speaker, one of the best encouragements for people to start a family and raise children is to have a job and the assurance that that job will be there and will pay more. If people have jobs and are trained as a result of the substantial increase in the moneys that we have made available, these are what are important to families. This will give people the confidence that there is a strong future for them.
Let me remind the Hon. Member-he is shaking his head. I do not think there are many people in the country shaking their heads, having seen a million and a half more people with jobs. I see the Hon. Member nodding. He agrees with me.
No.
There are a million and a half more people who have jobs today. That situation is giving people the confidence to build and grow and leave a better country for their children.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUBSIDIES TO VIA RAIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. One hundred and four years ago, under a Conservative Government, the last spike was driven to connect one end of this country to the other by rail. This morning the Minister of Transport delivered the last spike to the heart of VIA Rail by announcing the subsidy restrictions for the next number of years. Will the Minister confirm that the result of the subsidy level for 1993-94 is that VIA will only have sufficient funds to provide for those nine protected services, and therefore will not have the money to operate the Transcontinental, the Atlantic, the Windsor-Quebec City corridor and a number of other routes in this country? Will he confirm that that is the result of his decision?

subsubtopic: SUBSIDIES TO VIA RAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not confirm anything which has been said. TTiis morning, I gave some reference levels to the Board of Directors of VIA Rail which correspond to the reality
of the finances of this country, something we always have to keep in mind. I totally share the concern of the Minister of Finance. Transport Canada has to consider that also. We have set the new reference levels that the Government of Canada can provide to VIA Rail. Within those reference levels we would like to have proposals or options which will permit not only what the Board of Directors of VIA Rail want, but can afford. I believe that not only this Government but also the Member will have to consider the affordability of what we do in Canada with regard to transportation.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Since 1986 this Government has systematically undermined VIA Rail's ability to improve its service and to reduce the cost to taxpayers. It refused to give VIA the equipment it needed in order to turn it into a modem passenger rail system. It did not give it legislation. It has now fired the President of VIA Rail, who had the guts to oppose this Conservative Government's policy.
Will the Minister go back to Cabinet and say: "This does not make sense. I do not want to be the Minister who goes down in history as having destroyed passenger rail in this country''.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, if my friend wants me to talk about history, I will. It is true that 122 years ago this country was built by transportation-
Still is.

Can you listen, please, it is important. The decisions of today will be the past tomorrow. I do not want to give your children and my children a past made up of debts, deficit and inflation. I would not be proud of that kind of heritage for my children.

When one looks at transportation in this country, one recognizes that from an environmental point of view rail passenger transportation is the most environmentally sound opportunity we have.
Is the Minister suggesting that he is more willing to conserve the dollars and cents of the Minister of Finance than the environmental health of this countiy by forcing people to drive on highways instead of riding the rails? Is that what he is suggesting to the people of Canada?
May 3, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I think the point raised by the Hon. Member with respect to the environment deserves futher comment. What we are saying, what we said and what we intend to repeat to the corporation's board of directors, first of all, and to Canadians in general, is that we can no longer afford to invest $650 million annualy in a mode of transportation that is used by 3 to 5 per cent of the population. We must ensure that the modes of transportation used by Canadians have a financial structure that the Government can afford to support. We must not be unrealistic, Mr. Speaker. We can no longer afford what we have been paying during the past ten years in terms of subsidies to VIA Rail.

Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber

St. Barbe-Baie Verte):
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Transport. We noted last week some $500 million in cuts in VIA subsidies over the next five years. This morning the Minister of Transport fired the chief executive officer of VIA Rail because the chief executive officer believes that those cuts are inconsistent with the notion of maintaining a VIA Rail passenger service in this country.
Shame, shame!

My question to the Minister of Transport is a straightforward one. Is the Minister of Transport prepared to come clean with the people of Canada today and admit that the reason he fired the chief executive officer is that the Government of Canada has decided to close down VIA Rail's operations entirely in this country?
Hear, hear!
The Government of Canada does not have the courage to make a clean statement. The president left because the cuts are inconsistent with maintaining a rail passenger service in Canada.

Hear, hear!

May 3, 1989
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: GROWTH OF ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The Minister has stated that as a result of his Budget, growth in Canada's economy will slow and unemployment will increase next year. Analysts are now forecasting a drop in our economic growth of at least one full percentage point from over what it would have been without this Budget.
How can the Minister cut expenditures, raise taxes, keep interest rates high, and hope that the economy will somehow continue to grow at a healthy rate?
Will the Minister admit that his Budget is deliberately slowing growth in our economy, causing more inflation and causing yet more unemployment?

subsubtopic: GROWTH OF ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me quote a very learned observer who said:
The solution is quite simply for the Government to demonstrate a real ability to cut spending and to increase taxes-not very palatable ideas but necessary nevertheless-there are no magic solutions, MacLaren said.
That is a quote from the Hon. Member who has just asked the question. It is all very well to stand up on his hind legs and criticize, criticize, criticize, but Canadians are not going to be fooled. They can read what the Hon. Member said just three weeks ago and they know that the criticism is going to get nowhere.
What we are looking for in Canada today is an honest debate on the issues so we can understand where we are going as a country, where we are going as a people. I will answer the question if you will give me a little more time.

subsubtopic: GROWTH OF ECONOMY
speechtext: Where were you during the campaign?

subsubtopic: GROWTH OF ECONOMY
speechtext: Hon. Members opposite have been critical of the high interest rates in this country. They are saying we should get interest rates down. This is a Budget designed to get interest rates down.

subsubtopic: GROWTH OF ECONOMY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: GROWTH OF ECONOMY
speechtext: Now the Hon. Members say that that will not happen. This is designed to get interest rates down. I listen carefully to what Hon. Members say, and they say you cannot have it both ways. If we want to get interest rates down, we have to attack the fundamental causes of why interest rates are high. That is what this Budget does.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister says that we must get interest rates down. I agree with him, but he himself in his Budget is forecasting that interest rates will average 12 per cent this year. We are already into the fifth month of the year. Interest rates remain in excess of 12 per cent.
Given that the Minister predicts higher inflation while at the same time the Governor of the Bank of Canada has stated that inflation requires the imposition of yet higher interest rates, can the Minister explain somehow how anyone can believe that interest rates will drop before the end of this year?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member well knows, because I have another quote from him here, saying that lower inflation is essential to getting better productivity and lower interest rates. He is asking why we have not got interest rates down. The Budget was only presented last week. We cannot expect that just overnight, bang, things will happen, but the Hon. Member knows that the essential components of this Budget are designed to get interest rates down. We know the importance of getting interest rates down as demonstrated by the tremendous record of success we had in the last four years in which a million and a half jobs were created. Ibis is our objective and this Budget is designed to repeat that great record.
May 3, 1989

Oral Questions

subsubtopic: RENTAL RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION-CUTS IN SPENDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Housing. The Canadian Housing Renewal Association has said that the killing of the rental residential rehabilitation program will result in the decline of the living conditions of many low and moderate-income Canadians. This is the only major program that allows municipal and local Governments to upgrade substandard housing, to prevent conversions to high rise and high expense condominiums or to prevent demolition. What action will the Minister now take to help those thousands of Canadians, including children, who are caught in the housing crisis and who are being made homeless? Why not just keep this program?

subsubtopic: RENTAL RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION-CUTS IN SPENDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should know that I am as unhappy as he is, and in fact, the Government is as unhappy as he is with having to reduce spending on this particular social housing program. At the same time, the Hon. Member is aware and all Canadians are aware that a few years ago, 18 cents out of every dollar the Government took in went to pay for interest on the national debt. Last year, it was 31 cents out of every dollar. This year it will be 35 cents. Before very long, there will not be any social housing programs if that keeps up. In order to make sure that we are going to preserve social housing programs in Canada, we have to take action on that deficit.

subsubtopic: RENTAL RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION-CUTS IN SPENDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the rate this Government is going, there sure will not be any social programs left in this country.

My supplementary question is directed to the Minister. This Budget has cut needed social housing programs, has increased taxes on homes and has done everything to drive up interest rates rather than bring them down to make housing affordable. Can the Minister point to one single thing in this Budget that will actually provide Canadians with affordable housing?

Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member would examine the Estimates and the Budget very carefully, he would find that in fact, the Budget for social housing last year was $1.6 billion. This year it is $1.7 billion. There has actually been a $100 million increase in the social housing budget.

subsubtopic: BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. On a number of occasions in the past, the Prime Minister promised people in the forestry sector that he would give the industry the attention it deserved, considering its importance to Canada's economy. The Prime Minister also promised to establish a department that would be responsible for forestry. The Budget tells another story. It shows cutbacks of $28 million and 44 person years.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House whether the Prime Minister's commitments to the forestry sector were only empty promises? And how can he explain the cutbacks, in view of those commitments?

subsubtopic: BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be helpful to put the matter in the proper context. The Hon. Member is comparing what he has read in the Estimates with standards that were established by this Government and by this Prime Minister. There has been the restoration of the Canadian forest service to its rightful place as a full Department and accomplishments have been made in developing a forest sector strategy. There is a committee of Ministers that meets on a regular basis to plan future long-term integrated forest management policies that will not only preserve the commercial values of our forests but also the non-timber assets and will manage them properly. If the Hon. Member would read the information that I have sent him, he would know that there will not be a cut in the forestry budget but a significant increase once the establishment of the new Ministry and the separation from its previous Department is complete.

My supplementary question is directed to the Minister of State for Forestry. In the past, the Minister has stated how successfully the forest resource development agreements have functioned. Last year's Estimates for the agreements were $139 million. This year's Estimates reduce that amount by 25 per cent and next year's projections reduce that figure by 66 per cent. Can the Minister explain to the 5,000 people in New Brunswick who stand to lose their jobs if the agreements are not renegotiated why the agreements have been so severely cut? Moreover, does the Government have the intention of eliminating these agreements all together, and can he

May 3, 1989
Oral Questions
justify the loss of tens of thousands of jobs across Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Hon. Member has recognized the important achievements that have been made over the last four years. Hundreds of millions of seedlings have been planted, literally thousands of jobs have been created in silviculture and in forest farming. Hundreds of millions of hectares of land have been restocked and are treated effectively now, and of course, six of the agreements that have expired are presently being renegotiated with the provinces, and hopefully quite soon we will be in a position to enter into a new generation of those kinds of co-operative agreements that have proven so successful in the past.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL DRUG STRATEGY-ZERO TOLERANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question today is directed to the Minister of National Revenue.
I am sure that all Members of this House applaud the Minister's fight against the drug problem. However, the Minister was quoted in a number of articles last week as saying that the Government is seriously considering pursuing the policy of zero tolerance as a method of combating the drug problem in Canada.
Considering the less than successful record of this extremely controversial program in the United States, is the Minister so naive as to believe that zero tolerance alone will resolve the drug problem in Canada?
May 3, 1989

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: NATIONAL DRUG STRATEGY-ZERO TOLERANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, the Government is committed to the most comprehensive and broad program dealing with the serious drug problem, by virtue of the fact of the establishment of the national drug strategy.
To set the record straight, I will quote very briefly from what I said last week: "We will be looking at all options available to us including the pros and cons of zero tolerance". I will not be dissuaded by anybody anywhere in looking at every possibility to reduce the use of illegal drugs in Canada.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT SHARES IN AIRLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In privatizing Air Canada, the first annual meeting of Air Canada shareholders was told last week that the chairman and president of the airline were receiving interest-free loans to buy 275,000 shares at the original price of $8 per share. With these shares worth $11.50 today, the profits for these two people will be over $970,000, all based on interest-free loans.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance who votes the shares which the Government controls in Air Canada: Why was it that the Government did not vote its 55 per cent present share in Air Canada against these grossly generous benefits to two wealthy Canadians?
